General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great substantial-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • Industry observers note that the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach problems for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great substantial-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

Industry observers note that the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach problems for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

It has been revealed that three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential new line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

Industry observers note that they climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

It has been revealed that this significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

According to recent reports, one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

It has been revealed that the two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

According to recent reports, here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

Industry observers note that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

It has been revealed that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

According to recent reports, we had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive massive walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Industry observers note that are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Industry observers note that patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

In a recent development, the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

Industry observers note that you climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

According to recent reports, from there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

Industry observers note that all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

According to recent reports, how much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

Industry observers note that the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a latest route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

According to recent reports, your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

In a recent development, most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other massive-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Latest Update: Townsend Whelen’s Favorite Major Game Hunting Cartridges

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

  • He opined at length on the best cartridges for big game hunting, though he approached the topic with a characteristic open-mindedness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, townsend Whelen, who was one of Outdoor Life’s first shooting editors and one of the founders of the legendary gun maker and outfitter Griffin & Howe, wrote extensively about major game hunting from the early 1900s until his death in 1961. His articles on rifles, ballistics, cartridges, optics, and marksmanship have endured through the decades, thanks to his concise, informative prose that was based on years of practical experience as a hunter, competitive shooter, and career army officer.

He opined at length on the best cartridges for big game hunting, though he approached the topic with a characteristic open-mindedness. He was willing to consider and try newly introduced rounds as they became available, and loved to test out new equipment in the field and report on their results.

It has been revealed that I’ve unearthed Whelen’s favorite hunting cartridges by reading through his archived stories and books. One way to think of this list is as a snapshot of some key milestones in ballistic history, as well as an over-the-shoulder peek at the hunting rounds Whelen viewed as state of the art over his decades-long career. Many of his observations embody timeless wisdom and are still relevant today.

You’d think that among the cartridges he touted the .35 Whelen, which bears his name, would be included. After all, taking the .30/06 case—which was technologically advanced for the time—and necking it up for hard-hitting .358-caliber bullets was a winning combo.

It has been revealed that for not much increased recoil the .35 Whelen debuted bullets from 180- to 250-grains and promptly gained a reputation as a solid major-game killer. (Most .35 Whelen loads feature one of four bullet weights: 180, 200, 225 and 250 grains).

It has been revealed that whelen mentioned the round in passing—notably to give credit to James Howe (of Griffin & Howe) for designing it—and briefly touched upon others’ accounts of it in the field. But if he ever hunted with it, or even shot it much, he didn’t document the experience. As far as I’ve been able to learn, he never messed with the round in any meaningful way—other than doing some hand loading for it—and its exposure to the general reading public was through other writers of the time like Elmer Keith, who hunted with it extensively and was a fan of the 250-grain spitzers.

READ NEXT: Two Rifles for the Ages, Chambered in .35 Whelen.

Industry observers note that this blind spot to his eponymous cartridge extended to the .400 and .375 Whelens, which Howe developed at the same time, though they never caught on the way the .35 did. If I had to guess, I would say that Whelen’s modesty, refined upbringing (he came from Philadelphia aristocracy), and soldierly sense of decorum precluded him from overtly praising the cartridge, rather than the existence of some undisclosed antipathy toward it. To ballyhoo something bearing his name would be unseemly.

Recent findings suggest that the list of cartridges Whelen recommended for big game evolved over the years. His career spanned an era of explosive growth in cartridge and bullet development as well as the adoption of such marvels as telescopic sights.

For this reason, his earlier writings (from 1906 to the mid 1920s) prominently featured cartridges like the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army), the .30/30 W.C.F. (aka .30/30 Win.), 7mm Mauser, .250 Savage, and their peers. Later on, he became a fan of rounds such as the .270 Win., .257 Roberts, and .348 Winchester. Throughout his long career, however, he never wavered in his praise for the .30/06 and the .375 H&H (with some qualifiers) when the topic of major-game hunting turned to cartridge selection.

Industry observers note that whelen’s career as an authority on hunting and shooting marched in lockstep with the creation of the .30/06 and its rise to prominence. He was intimately familiar with the round and could rattle off technical details in his sleep concerning its history, refinements, the pros and cons of the numerous available loads, and its qualities on the battlefield and for hunting.

He worked with the cartridge both in his capacity as a sportsman and as an army officer—particularly after World War I when he transferred from Infantry to Ordnance, eventually becoming the commanding officer at Frankfort Arsenal and the director of research and development at the Springfield Armory.

In a recent development, he hunted extensively with the .30/06, killing all manner of significant game during his many adventures. One of his preferred projectiles was Western Cartridge Firm’s 180-grain open point boat tail bullet, with which he killed a grizzly bear, three moose, two caribou, two bighorn sheep, four mountain goats, and six deer.

He documented his experience with this bullet in particular because of occasional reports of 180-grain bullets failing on game. He wasn’t buying it.

Recent findings suggest that “There has never been even a suspicion of a failure on any of the game I have shot with it,” he wrote. “Many other sportsmen have had a similar experience.”.

Industry observers note that he found the bullet delivered good accuracy as well. “In my own rifle it was averaging about 2-inch groups at 100 and 4 inches at 200, and I got one moose killed clean at 325 yards and two goats killed likewise clean at 325 and 350 yards,” he noted.

On bigger game, many hunters gravitated toward 220- and 225-grain bullets back then, and the relative killing power of those bullets when compared to the wimpy 180s was a hot topic of discussion.

Whelen gives the heavier bullets their due, in particular the 220-grain soft points: “This bullet has made a very enviable reputation for fine killing power on larger game, and particularly on moose and Alaskan brown bear.”.

But when it came to terminal ballistics, a topic he was better versed in than most, he didn’t go along with the accepted wisdom that bigger meant better.

“It is generally supposed that the 220- and 225-grain bullets are more reliable killers on our larger game than those of 180 grains. I am not so sure of this,” he stated. “I would put them about on a par with the best of the 180-grain bullets up to 200 yards. Beyond that distance the trajectory of the 220 grain bullets becomes too curved to surely hit a deer or animals of that size.”.

In his opinion the effectiveness of those heavy bullets topped out around 225 yards, while the 180s and 172s could hit accurately and kill game to 350 yards.

It has been revealed that if he sounded like he held strong opinions on the .30/06 that’s because he did. He never hesitated to discuss—and defend—its effectiveness on game, but he also didn’t hold back critiques either.

Sources indicate that for instance, he took ammunition manufacturers to task in the 1930s for allowing the general quality of .30/06 ammo to slip. He had three “fine scope sighted rifles of Springfield, Winchester, and Remington makes” in his collection and gathered data that showed accuracy had fallen off from an average of 1 ¾ to 2 inches at 100 yards to 3-inch groups, while at 200 yards ammo that used to print 3 ½- to 4-inch groups now couldn’t shoot better than 7 inches.

READ NEXT: .30/06 Cartridge Review.

He felt ammo makers were neglecting the round in favor of newer offerings that were in the limelight and used the power of his platform at Outdoor Life and other publications to chastise those companies.

“With such ammunition a fine .30/06 rifle is no longer a 350-yard rifle, but rather a 225-yard arm for sure hits,” he mentioned.

The reason for his bluntness was that he hated the idea of the .30/06—which he mentioned is “never a mistake”—not living up to its potential as our best all-around big game cartridge.

Not many deer hunters today would list the .250 Savage among their top picks for whitetails—assuming they’re even aware of the cartridge’s existence. A lot of them would dismiss it as underpowered, though that would have come as a shock to Whelen. I guess whitetails have become more bulletproof since his day.

But when ballistic visionary Charles Newton created the .250-3000 in 1915 for the Savage 99 lever action, he gave American sportsmen their first high-power round capable of pushing a bullet at 3000 fps.

To be clear, Newton favored 100-grain bullets in the round with a muzzle velocity of 2800 fps, but Savage wanted to break the 3000-fps barrier and loaded it with 87-grainers which would do just that.

A lot of hunters jumped on the .250 Savage bandwagon and promptly demonstrated its worth in the woods.

“It has proved to be a very good deer cartridge,” Whelen wrote. Adding, “from hundreds of reports from the game fields it is quite clear that it gives a much larger percentage of instantaneous kills on deer with the first shot than does the .30/30 cartridge.”.

Whelen shot the .250 with 87- and 100-grain bullets, developing handloads for both. He favored the lighter bullet for small game, and the 100-grainers for varmints and deer.

READ NEXT: Best Deer Hunting Cartridges.

Industry observers note that when he first recommended the .250 Savage for deer, the .257 Roberts hadn’t been developed yet. By his own admission in later years, he felt anything the Savage could do the Roberts could do better.

“I think that a well-informed rifleman would hardly choose this cartridge because the .257 Roberts cartridge slightly excels it in every respect,” he mentioned.

I’m taking a bit of liberty with this one, as when Whelen wrote about mule deer earlier in his career he advocated the .30/30 W.C.F. as a minimum acceptable cartridge and, as he often did, defaulted to the .30/40 Krag with a 220-grain bullet as optimal. That mentioned, he did throw in a qualifier that any cartridges for other Western game would serve well on muleys.

According to recent reports, after the .270 Win. came on the scene, Whelen became a huge fan, calling it “one of the finest cartridges we have for American major game shooting—a very remarkable load.”.

He extolled the killing power and flat shooting characteristics of Winchester’s 130-grain spitzer bullet and described how a moose he shot with it “was killed more instantaneously than I have ever seen a moose killed before or since.”.

It has been revealed that his Winchester Model 54 was the most accurate big game rifle under 10 pounds he owned—capable of printing 10-shot groups at 100 yards measuring 1 7/8 inches, and 4-inch groups at 200. Relative to harder-kicking cartridges like the .30/06, the soft-shooting .270 lent itself to “fine practical accuracy.”.

As much as we link Jack O’Connor and the .270 Win., there’s little doubt as to Whelen’s perspective: “I think it is our best American major game cartridge in the hands of a rifleman who can avail himself of its flat trajectory and fine accuracy.”.

When Whelen joined the Army in the late 1890s prior to the Spanish American War, the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army and .30 US) was the standard matter round. It didn’t serve in that role long. It was adopted in 1892, replacing the .45/70 and then was ousted by the .30/03 (which later became the .30/06) in 1903.

Sources indicate that but like most cartridges employed by the military it became a hit with the sporting public, and as one of our first domestic smokeless powder rounds hunters took a shine to it. It shot a metal jacketed round nose 220-grain bullet at 2000 fps from a 30-inch barrel, which was hot stuff back then. In a carbine configuration with a 22-inch barrel, the velocity dropped to 1960 fps, which was still impressive for the time.

In 1899, a hunter killed the world-record Rocky Mountain elk with a .30/40 Krag, which cemented its reputation as good medicine for wapiti.

READ NEXT: Best Elk Hunting Cartridges.

Whelen liked the .30/40 Krag for elk, too. When he expressed this opinion in his book, American Significant Game Shooting, he felt it was the minimum one should attempt to hunt elk with and made a point of emphasizing the use of the 220-grain bullet rather than some of the lighter projectiles available.

That stated, in 1923 he gushed about the capabilities of the .30/40 Krag with a 180-grain open point bullet, declaring it “the most useful and all around successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman.”.

This round is all but forgotten today, having been consigned to the ballistic graveyard in 1936 when Winchester ditched it, along with the Model 1895 rifle that it was chambered in.

But from 1903, when it was developed, through the Roaring 20s the .35 Winchester had a respectable run as a substantial-game round that fell in between the .30/30 and the .405 Winchester, both of which are still produced today.

It has been revealed that like the .30/30 and .405, the .35 W.C.F. is a rimmed bottle-neck cartridge that shoots soft-pointed lead bullets from lever actions. Launching a 249-grain lead cast bullet at 1,500 fps would be plenty potent for moose, which is why Whelen mentioned this cartridge in American Significant Game Shooting.

READ NEXT: Best Moose Cartridges.

Of course, being a magnanimous sort, Whelen also lauded the .30/06, the .405, and later on cartridges like the .270 Win., as good options for moose hunters.

Sources indicate that nowhere does Whelen reveal his level-headed style of analysis more than when discussing hunting large bears. He loathed exaggeration as much as he loathed excessive recoil, so when discussing the best all-around bear cartridges he walks a fine line in terms of his recommendations.

Industry observers note that on the one hand, he discusses how tales of the ferocity of grizzly bears are vastly overstated—but without minimizing their toughness. “Today there is little danger attending the hunting of the grizzly for a fairly good shot, equipped with a modern rifle of fair killing qualities,” he stated. “However, a grizzly can carry away an awful amount of lead, and from the standpoint of obtaining the bear as well as for protection, a powerful rifle is desired.”.

What qualified as “powerful,” according to Whelen, were the .30/40 Krag, .30/06, .405 Winchester, .35 W.C.F., and the .375 H&H.

He rightly noted that the .375 H&H was a cut above those other rounds. At one point he described a scenario where when hunting large coastal brown bears in thick cover around salmon streams carrying a stopping cartridge like the .375 H&H was the way to go.

But he also understood the limitations of the round in terms of practical accuracy for most hunters.

According to recent reports, “The recoil is not severe to the thoroughly trained rifleman, but is rather heavy for the novice and the ordinary sportsman,” he said. He goes on, “I find that in many cases sportsmen have selected a rifle for this cartridge because they have had failures with the .30/06 cartridge. In almost every case of this kind, if we analyze the seeming failures with the latter cartridge we find that they are due either to a lack of skill in marksmanship, or else the wrong type of .30/06 cartridge was chosen for the game in question. The .375 Magnum cartridge will not in any sense make up for any lack of skill in marksmanship.”.

READ NEXT: Best Bear Hunting Cartridges.

He continues to hammer home this point, saying that a typical sportsman will be ill served trying to overgun for any animal, and is better off shooting a milder round with an appropriate bullet.

“It is certain that if one is a poor or only ordinary shot, he will shoot much worse with a rifle taking the .375 Magnum cartridge than with one less heavily loaded, due to recoil.”.

That perspective is as valid today as it was more than 70 years ago.

Sources indicate that this entry requires a bit of a caveat. First off, when Whelen first wrote about hunting black bears in American Significant Game Shooting, he didn’t offer a recommendation as to which cartridge to use. It is the only animal in that book that he declined to list one for.

Industry observers note that his reason for doing so was because he didn’t care to hunt them himself and wanted to see them protected by adequate game laws. At the time, bear hunting was largely unregulated and they were regarded as vermin. “The black bear is the only species of American game that I have not shot, and I never want to,” he mentioned.

“The black bear is the most amusing, ludicrous, human, and understandable of our wild animals, and in captivity it makes a most interesting pet…. It is entirely harmless, except on rare occasions, and it should be protected by proper game laws and permitted to survive,” he wrote.

That said, the book, which he did in conjunction with the Western Cartridge Tech giant, had a picture of the above-mentioned .35 Winchester Cartridge under the black bear entry, which was a good all-around significant-game woods cartridge.

The rise in popularity of the .35 Remington no doubt hastened the .35 Winchester’s demise. It was initially offered in Remington’s Model 8 autoloading rifles and was later chambered in Remington Model 14 and 141 pump actions and the Model 30 bolt gun. Marlin started chambering it in their lever-actions in 1953.

All this is to say that Whelen recognized the capabilities of the .35 Remington as an all-around option for deer, bear, and other animals.

“It is a good cartridge of moderate power and range for use on all American substantial game. It kills very well at medium ranges, being in this respect much superior to cartridges of the .30/30 class,” he said.

Industry observers note that he felt the cartridge was a good match for the Remington Model 141 in particular. “Deer will be killed much more quickly and reliably than with the other cartridges adapted to this rifle, and (in the rifle it) is by no means out of the running for moose, elk, or large bear.”.

Among all the cartridges Whelen spent time with, the quarter-bore “Bob” was his all-time favorite. He was in touch with Ned Roberts during the development of the .257 Roberts in the mid-1920s and encouraged him to call it the “.25 Roberts” in light of the effort he put into creating the round, which is based on a necked-down 7×57 Mauser.

“I think that no man has ever spent so much time in perfecting a cartridge as Mr. Roberts spent on this one,” Whelen wrote.

Whelen who was an avid varmint shooter and one of the driving forces behind the development of benchrest shooting, loved small, accurate cartridges so it is no wonder he took to the Roberts when it was introduced.

He favored 100-grain bullets for their flat shooting and hard-hitting capabilities on woodchucks out to 300 yards and on crows to 200 yards.

“I do not know of a finer long range varmint cartridge than this, particularly with hand loaded cartridges,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that he didn’t feel it was limited to popping chucks, however. “It has been proved innumerable times that the full charged cartridges loaded with 100- and 117-grain bullets give excellent results on deer, and we therefore here have a most excellent all-around cartridge which a rifleman can use all year round for small game, varmints, and target, and then take into the substantial woods after deer in the fall,” he said, adding that other than for moose and elk it was a good option for other game, including antelope.

Read Next: Best Antelope Cartridges.

Because of its light recoil, relatively soft report, excellent accuracy, and—for the time—wide bullet selection he stated it would get the nod as the one cartridge he’d pick if could only shoot one.

“I consider it a very fine cartridge, and if I had of necessity to confine myself to one rifle only I would choose it in this caliber,” he said.

In a recent development, whelen didn’t mince words when it came to hunting sheep and goats. He knew through first-hand experience how challenging those animals are, both in terms of the terrain that needed to be traversed to get to them and the difficult shots a hunter was often confronted with.

“The hunting and stalking of them is so difficult that the head of a massive ram killed by fair stalking is the most prized trophy that can fall to the rifle of the American hunter,” he said. “Often the stalk ends with the hunter quite a long distance from his game with no chance of getting closer unobserved…for this reason a rifle adapted to a cartridge of very high velocity and extreme accuracy at long ranges is most desirable.”.

The two cartridges he touted as most capable for this work were the “.30 caliber Model 1906” shooting a 180-grain “Open Point” and the 7mm Mauser shooting a 139-grain open point.

In his personal 7mm Mauser he was able to swap between 175-grain expanding bullets for large game and the 139s when it came time to go after deer, sheep, goats, antelope and varmints.

When zeroed with the 139s at 100 yards, the 175s shot to point of aim at 200 yards, giving him the confidence to swap ammo as needed on the fly.

But he warned his readers not to count on that trick working in their personal guns.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes such a combination can be worked out for certain rifles, and for some it cannot be accomplished. It is not so much a matter of cartridge, caliber, or make of rifle, as how the individual barrel vibrates with each load.”.

Industry observers note that one thing that’s clear to me is that Whelen would have been a fan of the 6.5 Creedmoor. He loved mild, accurate, and effective cartridges, particularly when loaded with the proper bullets, and didn’t hesitate to employ them on massive game.

It shouldn’t come as a shock then to see him sing the praises of the 6.5x54mm Mannlicher Schoenauer as a good choice for caribou.

“Caribou are often found in open or partly open country, and the careful stalking necessary to bring them to bag, with attention to wind, sight, and hearing, make their pursuit a splendid sport,” he mentioned. “As they are often in localities where it is impossible to approach very closely, a rifle which is effective at long range is very desirable, usually one firing a military or semi-military type cartridge.”.

He states that caribou deserve a cartridge along the lines of what one would use for elk and lists the .30/06, 7mm Mauser, and 6.5mm Mannlicher as examples—all of which were standard glitch military rounds at the time.

Industry observers note that whelen’s eclectic and open-minded approach to cartridges was a defining characteristic of his. So narrowing down a list of his favorite rounds is a bit tricky.

On the one hand, in 1923 he called the .30/40 Krag the “most useful” and “successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman” that “will kill with a single shot any game in America.” He supported that statement with anecdotes of his own success with the .30/40 Krag in the field, including a one-shot instant kill on an 18-foot crocodile. Fast forward 17 years to 1940 and he doesn’t even mention the round in his thick tome, The Hunting Rifle.

That was in part a function of the rapid pace of small arms and ammunition development at the time. Whelen’s job was to be on the cutting edge of all things ballistic, and he refused to stick with something out of a sense of nostalgia.

In a recent development, that said, having read much of what Whelen wrote I’ve aimed to do him justice with the rounds I picked. All of the cartridges mentioned are ones he bestowed his imprimatur upon, though I will be curious to see what other fans of “Townie”—as he was called by his friends—think his favorites would have been.

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

According to recent reports, with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Sources indicate that last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

The skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

Industry observers note that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police noted the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Industry observers note that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

The avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

In a recent development, the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

In a recent development, fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the massive powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them proposal to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) demonstrates low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

According to recent reports, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps highlights remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

According to recent reports, today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police revealed that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

Climbers Forge Upcoming Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • According to recent reports, expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

According to recent reports, expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

Siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

In a recent development, sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist claims the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

Sources indicate that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast declared a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

It has been revealed that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

In a recent development, the sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

Tech Report: Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Sources indicate that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Sources indicate that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

Sources indicate that it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

At first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

Recent findings suggest that A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Recent findings suggest that yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

Industry observers note that according to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Industry observers note that tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold new routes here.

According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

#159639. Bears, Moldy Gear & Navigation Mishaps: My First Solo Backpacking Adventure on the Florida Trail

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2586 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Bears, Moldy Gear & Navigation Mishaps: My First Solo Backpacking Adventure on the Florida Trail

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something empowering about stepping into the wilderness alone, knowing that whatever happens, you’re the one who has to figure it out.
  • Recent findings suggest that for my first-ever solo backpacking trip, I set out to hike a 60 mile section of the Florida Trail through the Ocala National Forest and Juniper Wilderness Area.
  • Recent findings suggest that what I didn’t anticipate was just how much the trail would throw at me in four short days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Follow Colleen Wilson and Lane Early.

There’s something empowering about stepping into the wilderness alone, knowing that whatever happens, you’re the one who has to figure it out.

Recent findings suggest that for my first-ever solo backpacking trip, I set out to hike a 60 mile section of the Florida Trail through the Ocala National Forest and Juniper Wilderness Area. I’ve spent thousands of miles backpacking alongside Lane, often leaning on his experience and confidence in the backcountry. This time, I wanted to put my own skills to the test. I wanted to see what it felt like to navigate the challenges, make the decisions, and handle whatever the trail threw at me without someone else to lean on.

Recent findings suggest that what I didn’t anticipate was just how much the trail would throw at me in four short days. What started as a simple, well-planned backpacking trip, rapidly turned into some of the most challenging days I’ve ever experienced on the trail and with so many things going wrong.

Between a mold-infested sleeping bag, curious black bears (including a face-to-face encounter), countless tick and chigger bites, sleepless cold nights, unexpected detours due to navigational mistakes, and a few genuinely beautiful stretches of wilderness, this trip turned into an adventure I won’t soon forget.

More importantly, it built a confidence in myself that I hadn’t fully tapped into before. I discovered that I really enjoy the solitude, the independence, and the sense of empowerment that comes with figuring things out on my own.

My dad dropped me off at Rodman Dam around 1:30 p.m., after we first cached some water at the County Road 316 crossing. I headed north through the tall longleaf pine forests, with sections of lightly overgrown trail scattered throughout the afternoon.

Recent findings suggest that I encountered only two northbound hikers during the first few miles, and they would turn out to be the only hikers I’d see over the entire 60-mile stretch. Within the first hour, I also came across some fresh bear scat, a friendly little reminder that I was no longer walking through the Florida I was accustomed to growing up here in the Sunshine State.

Sources indicate that I made it about seven miles before finding a spot off-trail to set up camp around 5:30 p.m. I could hear ATVs riding throughout the area, and rather than push on toward the campground, I decided to call it a day and settle in so I could enjoy some reading in the tent before dinner.

That’s when things started getting interesting.

Recent findings suggest that after setting up camp, I discovered that my sleeping bag had developed mold all over it since the last time I’d used it. Awesome.

So, I laid the bag outside on the ground beside my tent to start drying before I would pack it away in my backpack and hope it wouldn’t get cold enough that I would actually need it.

In a recent development, after prepping dinner in my tent, which consisted of cold soaking some ramen in a talenti ice cream container, I heard sniffing around my tent. I turned around and found myself practically eye-to-eye with a black bear investigating my moldy sleeping bag.

In a recent development, my first reaction was to yell, “Get out of here bear!” Making my voice deeper and louder with each attempt at repeating this chant. It jumped back, startled by my yelling.

In a recent development, I grabbed my bear spray, got out of the tent, and yelled until it eventually wandered off. It kept stopping to look back at me curiously before disappearing out of sight. Not exactly the wildlife encounter I’d been hoping for on my first solo night.

I packed up my food and ate dinner a good distance away from camp, making sure to keep everything bear-proofed.

According to recent reports, naturally, I was now convinced the bear would be returning for a second visit. Like they do in every story you hear about when a person is attacked by a bear and decides to sleep with their food even after a bear sniffs their campsite the first time.

Sources indicate that then I discovered it wasn’t just my sleeping bag. My sleeping bag liner and pillow were all covered in mold, too. This was going to be a long first night.

It has been revealed that at this point, I wasn’t going to be using any of this gear and all I had to rely on was my sleeping pad and a makeshift pillow made from a stuff sack and anything I could find in my pack to give it some volume. I could only hope that all the clothing layers in my pack would be enough to get me through the night as I layered them on, one-by-one.

And because apparently everything comes in threes, I found a tiny tick on my leg while changing clothes for bed.

I crawled into my tent, listened to coyotes howling in the distance, and tried to settle in with a book. Their howls seemed to get closer as the evening went on. Each sound startled me awake, thinking the bear was returning to take me out.

In a recent development, at this point I was questioning even sticking out this backpacking trip and considering calling it quits by calling for a pickup. It was going to be a tougher few days than I’d anticipated. But, as they say, “Never quit on a bad day.” I’d try to make it through the night and assess things tomorrow.

There were three main reasons. First, my sleeping setup was covered in mold, and although I initially refused to use it, I eventually got cold enough to give in. I ended up wearing practically every layer I had in my pack, including three pairs of socks, before finally pulling the moldy sleeping bag over my feet.

Second, every unfamiliar noise had me convinced a bear was circling my tent.

And third, the ATV riders and country boys in trucks seemed to be going strong until around midnight.

Needless to say, I was ready to get moving at sunrise.

Industry observers note that the morning brought some beautiful stretches of trail, although there were plenty of overgrown and thorny sections to navigate. At one point, I heard what I believe was another bear charging onto the trail behind me. I made my way rapidly toward the busy traffic of CR 316, where I felt a little more comfortable.

It has been revealed that I accidentally walked about 0.4 miles past Store 88 where I planned to charge my phone which I needed for navigation and had to backtrack. While there, I met a 70-year-old British guy named Calvin Kline, who was working on fixing up the old place alongside his elderly dog. We chatted for about 45 minutes about life experiences and places we have traveled that we both had in common. One of those unexpected trail encounters that makes long-distance hiking so interesting.

After lunch, I pushed on for another five or so miles until reaching the Salt Springs blue-blaze junction. There was a bench where I’d planned to take my dinner break, but instead I discovered something much more key: a campground another 6.5 miles ahead that had bear boxes.

I desperately needed a bear box.

It was already a little after 5 p.m., but I knew I needed to make it there. I pushed through the remaining miles and arrived shortly after 8 p.m. and hiking by headlamp.

Recent findings suggest that I set up camp, secured my food in the bear box, and finally felt like I could relax a little. Dinner was cold-soaked ramen that I’d started preparing 6.4 miles earlier.

After dinner I tried to access the food in the bear box and the doors were jammed. Great. Now I would really need to pull the plug and call for a pickup in the morning. No food means no fuel to keep hiking, unless I could find someone camping in the area that could help me get the doors unjammed. Eventually I broke into the box and was relieved that I didn’t have to quit, again.

There were other campers around, a secure place to store my food, and a much better chance of getting some sleep.

After the previous night, it felt like a luxury to not have to sleep with my food in this heavily bear dense area.

I woke up at sunrise and headed out through a beautiful prairie section before entering one of my favorite stretches of the entire trip: the Juniper Wilderness Area.

It has been revealed that the trail through the forest was absolutely gorgeous. It was one of those sections that makes you forget about all the little inconveniences of backpacking and reminds you exactly why you spend so much time out here.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, I made my way to Juniper Springs Recreation Area, where I had planned a seven-mile kayak float. The current was ripping pretty good and with all the down trees it made for quite the obstacle course. At one point I was pinned in between a down log and some overhanging brush and ended up snapping my sunglasses into two pieces.

Recent findings suggest that A few miles into the float I met Bryan, who works for the local kayaking organization. We ended up floating about 3.5 miles together, chatting and swapping stories about Florida and it’s wild backcountry along the way. It was a nice change of pace from the solitude of the trail.

In a recent development, I camped at the recreation area that evening for $50, charged my electronics, and met a couple from Ohio who work for the North Country Trail. We spent a while chatting and they were eager to ask questions about my experience on The Florida Trail so far as they were day hiking sections of it during their visit to the state.

It was a much-needed reset after two eventful days in the woods.

I woke up at sunrise with the goal of hiking the remaining miles to Alexander Springs, where my parents were scheduled to pick me up.

I believe I had around 18 miles left.

Industry observers note that the morning started off well, but somewhere around lunchtime, I managed to make a pretty significant navigation mistake. I sat down on a log to eat, got back on trail, and somehow ended up hiking in the wrong direction, back toward a road I’d already passed.

Industry observers note that by the time I realized what I’d done, I’d walked 1.7 miles in the wrong direction. That meant an additional 3.4 miles of bonus hiking for the day.

Sources indicate that exactly what I needed. Plus, the trail had was quite overgrown and I was covered in spiky stickers.

In a recent development, I picked up the pace to make sure I’d still reach my parents on time. Along the way, I continued seeing plenty of bear scat, including some that looked particularly fresh.

Then I came upon a very large black bear directly on the trail.

It has been revealed that I startled it, and it took off running with such incredible speed and force that, for a split second, I was terrified it was charging straight toward me. Thankfully, it veered into the woods and disappeared.

I spent the next mile or so periodically shouting, “HEY BEAR!” with my bear spray close at hand.

For the remainder of the hike, I found myself constantly scanning every turn in the trail, anticipating another bear around the next corner.

In a recent development, it was an interesting balancing act. I needed to speed hike to make my scheduled pickup time, but I also didn’t want to move so swiftly as to startle another bear.

Eventually, I made it to the forest road and found a log to sit on while waiting for my parents.

I was exhausted, but incredibly proud of myself.

I had navigated the trail, dealt with unexpected challenges, made mistakes and figured them out, and pushed through situations that would have been much easier with someone else there to lean on.

In a recent development, and honestly? I already felt ready to keep going.

But those miles would have to wait. I couldn’t stand the thought of spending another night in my moldy sleeping bag, especially without a bear canister or bear box to store my food.

Four days was enough for this adventure.

One of the things I appreciated most about this trip was how it changed my perspective on Florida.

For a long time, I associated Florida with bustling cities, traffic, and endless stretches of concrete. I spent time commuting an hour to work in Miami, and my idea of escaping the city was taking a scenic backroad on a weekend drive to my home in Fort Lauderdale.

I never really appreciated just how much wilderness existed beyond the interstates connecting Florida’s major cities.

Industry observers note that after walking more than 500 miles through Florida’s wilderness over the last several years, I’ve come to see the state in an entirely different light. There are enormous stretches of forests, springs, prairies, rivers, and protected wilderness that feel worlds away from the metropolitan areas most people associate with Florida.

Industry observers note that there’s still a wild Florida out there. You just have to get off the interstate to find it.

More than anything, this trip gave me a upcoming appreciation for what I’m capable of on my own.

I’ve spent so much of my backpacking experience alongside Lane, and while I’ve learned an incredible amount from him, I think there’s something vital about stepping away from the comfort of having someone more experienced beside you.

Recent findings suggest that you have to trust your own judgment. You have to make your own decisions. When something goes wrong, there’s nobody to immediately turn to for reassurance or a solution.

According to recent reports, I loved the solitude. I loved making my own decisions, moving at my own pace, and having the freedom to experience the wilderness on my terms.

And perhaps most importantly, I came away with a confidence that I hadn’t realized I was missing.

Industry observers note that I don’t need to wait for someone else to be available to go backpacking. I don’t need someone else’s experience to validate my own abilities.

And I have a feeling this won’t be my last solo adventure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

The storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

In a recent development, driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Industry observers note that up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better tech giant but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

In a recent development, gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

The reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the newly introduced windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

It’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

#159635. Tech Report: How to Sharpen an Axe Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1542 w)

Tech Report: How to Sharpen an Axe Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Many people have heard the story about two woodcutters chopping trees in the forest.
  • According to recent reports, A sharp axe will have less glancing blows, cut deeper, and cut faster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Many people have heard the story about two woodcutters chopping trees in the forest. One chops and chops and chops without stopping, while the other takes breaks frequently, but still manages to chop more wood. That’s because while the second woodcutter was “on break” he was sharpening his axe. Now, lots of corporate types use this story to try to teach something about productivity, or whatever, but the only real takeaway is that a sharp axe translates to less hard work.

According to recent reports, A sharp axe will have less glancing blows, cut deeper, and cut faster. I’m not interested in banging a dull hunk of metal into a tree for 15 minutes when I could get it done with a sharp axe in less than five. So, sharp axe good, dull axe bad. But how do you get your axe nice and sharp and ready to do some real work? Believe it or not, it’s not that hard, and it doesn’t require expensive tools. Here’s a step-by-step guide on how to sharpen an axe.

Industry observers note that for this method, you really only need two tools. A flat file, and a “puck” style sharpening stone. The file should be a Mill Bastard file. These are commonly available at any hardware store, and if you get your technique correct, you don’t actually need a puck afterward. An 8” or bigger file makes this easier, but you can get the job done with a smaller 4” or 6” file. I sharpened my axe for this tutorial with a flat file for leveling chainsaw guide teeth, just to show that it can be done with a small file. (Plus my bigger file is getting dull and needs replacing).

After you’re done with the file, you can move on to really honing and sharpening the edge with a puck-style sharpening stone. I use stones from Straight Grain Supply because they are dual grit, and the rubber band makes for a good grip. The stones come in a variety of grits, and can be used alone without a file if you like. I use both because the file removes damage faster, and the pucks give a finer edge with the higher grits. For these stones, I keep a bowl of water and an old toothbrush handy. Letting them sit in water before sharpening helps to keep them from getting clogged up with metal particles. A quick scrub with the toothbrush and some water helps keep them clean and cutting properly and it extends their effective life.

Sources indicate that if you have a vise, that can be helpful if there is damage that needs to be sharpened out, but it’s not necessary. If you don’t have a vise, having a longer file is much more vital. More on that later. The last thing you will need is a dull axe. I used my “beater” axe for this story. It’s been used as a wedge and it’s been beaten and deformed. It has smashed more than a couple rocks while taking out roots. It had some serious damage, so I thought it would be useful to show how effective the file is. As a final note, I recommend wearing a pair of work gloves for this because your hands and fingertips will be very close to the edge.

In a recent development, first, you will take your file and set your edge angle and thin out the cheek of the axe. The cheek is the portion of the blade just behind the edge. You can thin this out if you want the axe to chop deeper into the wood. If you have to bring the edge back for significant damage, you should file the cheeks down a bit to keep the cutting performance. Make sure you are sharpening the whole bevel, not just a tiny portion near the apex of the edge. With a longer file, you can ball up an old rag or t-shirt and put it on the axe head and rest the tip of the file on it as you make your cuts with the back of the file. Make the rag thick or thinner so you can match the angle of the bevel. The rag acts as a pivot point for the file and allows you to keep pressure on the axe head so it won’t move around.

Industry observers note that with a shorter file, this method won’t work, and a vise really comes in handy. For wood handled axes, rubber jaw protectors, rags, or leather can be used to protect the wood in the vise.

In a recent development, pull your file across the edge from one end of the blade to the other. These files don’t just cut with the file moving from tip to handle, they cut laterally as well. You will feel the file bite into the material. Lift the file and go back and make another lateral pull.

Sources indicate that make passes until all damage is removed, and you feel a burr on the entire edge. Flip it over and do the same thing to the other side. After you have apexed the edge on both sides, you should have a pretty sharp axe, and you can stop here if you want. With just a file, you can achieve a great working edge. But, I like my stuff really sharp, so I continue on to the stones.

Industry observers note that once you have removed the heavy damage and re-profiled the edge with your file, you can refine the edge with progressively finer grit stones. If you don’t have a file, you can use a coarse stone to profile the edge, but it will generally take more time, especially if there are some deeper chips or rolls in the edge.

After your stones have soaked in the water a bit, “scrub” the entire beveled edge with the puck using small circular motions to refine it. Hold the puck with your fingertips and keep them away from the edge. You will see the scratch pattern from the stone taking away the tooling marks from the file.

According to recent reports, give your stone a dip in the water every so often to keep it clean. When you have removed the marks from the file on the whole edge, repeat for the other side. Then, get the next grit stone, and repeat this process on each side. Scrub until the scratch pattern from the previous grit stone is gone. I usually use the medium grit after the file work and progress to a fine grit. Straight Grain Supply makes two-sided stones in 80/220 grit, 220/400 grit, and 220/600 grit. I use the 220 grit and then progress to my 400 grit side. I have used the 80 grit side for damage before, and it will remove material fairly rapidly, but I still prefer a file for initial shaping. After you have done both sides with medium and fine grit, your axe should be ready to go, and will be taking on a nice shiny, somewhat polished appearance. If you have a leather strop, you could make a few passes on that just to remove any small burr that might remain and further polish and refine the edge, but the bur will be gone on the first chop or two anyway. I strop mine because I have one, and I like the edge to be shiny after I’m done. If you want the best edge possible, take your time with these steps. It will be worth it when you start chopping.

Industry observers note that once you profile and remove damage on an axe, maintaining that sharp edge shouldn’t take much effort at all. After each use, take a minute or so and hone each side with your finest grit puck stone before you put the axe away, and you will generally be able to go a long time before you have to sharpen it again. Now, if you happen to hit a rock or nail or something else that damages the edge beyond small nicks, then you will have to go through the whole process again. A little maintenance after each use will keep your axe cutting well between sharpening, and prolong the life of the axe head. If you maintain it with a file every time, you will remove more material than needed and wear out the bit of the axe sooner. An ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure.

Read Next: Best Camping Axes, Tested and Reviewed.

A little time spent learning how to sharpen an axe will pay dividends when it comes time for chopping. For me, few things are as frustrating as a tool not performing the way it is supposed to. The thing is, you might not think your axe is even dull, but if you take the time to sharpen it, you will be amazed at the difference in cutting performance. Invest a little in sharpening and save a bunch of hard work down the road. Keep your axes sharp.

Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.

According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.

Recent findings suggest that he was found dead the next morning. Past Mera Peak climbers have suggested on social media that it was unusual to overnight in the high camp after summiting so early in the day.

Industry observers note that his body was evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu for an autopsy. The cause of death remains undetermined. An initial report raised the possibility of altitude-related illness or a cardiac event, but neither has been established medically.

According to recent reports, skidmore previously summited Lobuche Peak in 2024, according to the Everest Chronicle and the Italian Alpine Club’s publication Lo Scarpone. So he had previous Himalayan climbing experience above 6,000m.

The Himalayan Database does include Mera Peak, but its coverage of popular trekking peaks is selective. However, it notes that since 2018, four people have died on Mera Peak, not counting Skidmore.
