#159597. A Thanksgiving Blizzard Pushed Big Mule Deer Off the Mountain — and Down to Us

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3183 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

A Thanksgiving Blizzard Pushed Big Mule Deer Off the Mountain — and Down to Us

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 glitch of Outdoor Life.
  • For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S.
  • Sources indicate that but following the trail wasn’t always easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Buck and The Great Gray Owl,” appeared in the November 1972 glitch of Outdoor Life.

For at least a mile, I had trudged along a U.S. Forest Service trail to avoid hunting through the dense evergreen woods on both sides. There the trees sagged under heavy burdens of snow, and to brush against just one branch was to release a load of it down the back of my neck.

Sources indicate that but following the trail wasn’t always easy. In places the blaze marks were obliterated by snow that a high wind had plastered against the tree trunks, and here and there drifts were piled waist-high. Slogging through such deep wet snow can take the joy out of deer hunting, so I decided to head back for the warmth and comfort of the ranch. I elected to take a shortcut rather than to retrace my steps, and that decision proved to be a mistake.

According to recent reports, my shortcut led down and around a slope, then crossed an old burned area, now grown up in a thicket, where the newly introduced snow covered a nightmare of crisscrossed deadfalls. Before I reached the far side of the burn, I tripped many times and was wet from chest to toes. I swore out loud the last time I fell, and in that instant three does suddenly sprung from their beds in the snow and fled downhill.

The does did not bounce away in the characteristic stiff-legged manner of mule deer. Instead they hesitated and floundered, now and then up to their bellies in the snow. I threw the rifle to my shoulder and could easily have shot all three, so slow was their progress. But the purpose of my trip was to bag one good buck, and I had a few more days to hunt.

Back in camp, I found George Smith and John Moxley propping wet boots close to a cast-iron stove to dry while a pot of coffee brewed on top.

“Did you see any game?” I asked.

“Not even a fresh track,” George answered.

“We may have started this hunt too late,” John added.

I almost had to agree with John — the three does were the only deer I had seen since arriving at George Smith’s Canyon Creek Ranch. For years George has been guiding hunters from this ranch, located in the Pioneer Mountains of the Beaverhead National Forest, about 17 miles of steep winding road from Melrose, Montana. When John and I couldn’t make our annual Western hunt in time for the October opening of the major-game season, George suggested that we hold off until the season’s last week, which would be the last week in November.

“By that time,” he had written, “the massive bucks should be down low and we can have a real trophy hunt. Besides, all my guests will have gone home for Thanksgiving, so Bob and I can join you.”.

Bob is my youngest son, and he was working for the Smith family during the season as a guide and wrangler.

The blueprint sounded perfect to John and me. John is from Ohio, and I had recently moved from Ohio to Wyoming.

Industry observers note that on a crisp bright day in November — perfect weather for major-game hunting — I met John at the airport in Butte, Montana. We picked up some supplies and then drove the 60 miles to Canyon Creek Ranch. We arrived well after dusk under a still-clear sky.

In a recent development, I’d never felt more optimistic about starting a hunt. But two things did bother me. First, we did not see any deer in the headlights of our vehicle on the drive to the ranch. Second, after our arrival George mentioned seeing a great gray owl around the ranch buildings. In that region the great gray is a rare visitor, and according to George it arrives only ahead of a storm.

“The last gray owl I saw,” George recalled, “came just before the worst winter storm in my memory hit this place.”.

Sources indicate that late that night, snow began to fall and a violent wind came up. The snow didn’t stop until more than a foot of white covered the high country — about 7,000 feet at the Canyon Creek Ranch — and the temperature plunged to zero. We did very little hunting, and it was unsuccessful.

“The deer have either bedded down until the blast passes,” George explained, “or moved down to where the snow isn’t so deep. We’ll have to wait and see.”.

At first the waiting wasn’t too bad. I hadn’t seen Bob or George for a year, and we had plenty of stories to swap in the snug ranch atmosphere. Besides, there was a Thanksgiving banquet to cook and eat. But eventually I got restless and wanted to start hunting in spite of the conditions. The result was that we left a good many bootprints in the deep snow without covering much distance or seeing any deer or even any game sign.

According to recent reports, the morning after I saw the does, I started out early. The wind had stopped blowing, but visibility was still poor. Gray clouds hung in the canyons and close to the wooded slopes so that long-range scanning with binoculars was seldom possible. One very effective tactic for hunting in good snow cover in mountainous country is to carefully glass all slopes, particularly south slopes, for game that stands out sharply against the white. The clouds ruled out that tactic.

But the day didn’t pass without excitement. I had crossed a steep draw and, on reaching level ground on the far side, had paused to catch my breath. A moment later I heard animals crashing toward me through an evergreen thicket up ahead. My heart began to pound. I flipped off the safety on my Model 700 Remington 7 mm. Magnum and held the rifle ready. A cow moose followed by a calf stomped into the open and crossed my path without even a sidelong glance in my direction. It was quite a surprise to see them so far from more-typical moose habitat.

According to recent reports, bob had good news back at the ranch that night. He had scouted in another direction and found many tracks.

It has been revealed that “They seem to be paralleling Canyon Creek, heading down toward the old ghost camp,” Bob said. “If the snow’s thinner, we might find them there tomorrow.”.

According to recent reports, the next morning was bitterly cold. We gathered in the ranch kitchen and huddled around the cook stove while George carved thick strips of bacon from a slab and mixed up a large bowl of sourdough pancake batter. It is a standard practical joke around Canyon Creek to conceal a round sheet of cardboard inside some unsuspecting diner’s pancake and then watch him try to cut it with a fork. George pulled the trick on John, and we had a good laugh before beginning a cold day.

In a recent development, it was possible to drive our four-wheel-drive rig partway to where Bob had found sign the day before. We parked our vehicle beside a small tributary of Canyon Creek, now almost completely frozen, and followed it on foot to an open meadow bordered by a wooded slope. There we found Bob’s tracks as well as deer tracks that had been made since his reconnaissance. It was soon evident that a herd of deer had fed along the meadow’s edges; in windswept places they had pawed circular areas free of snow to get at the vegetation underneath. But apparently the deer hadn’t lingered long, and their tracks disappeared in many different directions.

“Our best bet,” George said, “is to go separate ways and see what we find.”.

Because George knew the country best, he took a more complicated route, which led through heavy cover, wound around a mountainside, and nearly dead-ended at a steep rocky cliff. He figured that game might be bedded on top or near the face of the cliff.

John and I proceeded together until the meandering tracks appeared to divide into two small herds. Then we separated, planning to meet late in the day on an unimproved road far below.

Recent findings suggest that one set of the tracks I followed was very large, and I concentrated on it. I walked parallel to the buck’s path on the downwind side while watching far ahead for a glimpse of the animal. That technique had worked well for me on other hunts, and it might work again.

In a recent development, I was so intent on following the buck that I almost stumbled over a bedded doe. She went flying in a cloud of snow down the slope. Then, before my hands were steady again, a shot cracked in the distance. The shot spooked a second deer about 150 yards to my right. I saw the animal for only an instant and couldn’t tell whether it was my buck. But when I hurried back to the buck’s trail, I found the spot where he had suddenly shifted into high gear.

For the rest of the day I stillhunted slowly but got no action. I was optimistic, however, for at last we were in deer country.

The shot I’d heard was George’s. He had broken the ice. About a mile from where he’d left John and me, he’d noticed that the tracks of the largest deer became more meandering — often an indication that a deer is seeking a good place to bed. George slowed his own pace accordingly, stopping often to scan thoroughly every bit of mountain terrain in front of him. This is the simplest and oldest of all mule-deer-hunting strategies, and once again it paid off.

Just before George reached a small draw, he stopped. Soon he saw a shape that put him on alert. On the slope slightly above him was the outline of a buck’s rack, somewhat obscured by a screen of brush. In the next moment the deer was on its feet and running. But it was slowed by snow, and it hadn’t gone more than 20 feet when George drilled a shot through the lungs. He found the animal dead 50 yards from where it had been hit.

In a recent development, the buck was an old, heavy five-pointer (Western count) with unusually heavy beams. It was a trophy that even an old-timer in the Montana Rockies could brag about. The buck, even when field-dressed, was a terrible weight to drag to the nearest pickup point. Without the slippery snow and all-downhill going, we would have needed a packhorse or two for the job.

Sources indicate that but the day produced more than a trophy mule deer for George. It also revealed that deer were moving from the high country into lower ranges where food was more available. The farther we had hunted that day, the more fresh tracks we had encountered. John reported jumping 12 deer from a sheltered meadow that, from the amount of tracks and digging in the snow, resembled a livestock pasture. None of the deer had the kind of rack that John was looking for, but his gloom early in the trip had been replaced by enthusiasm.

“Tomorrow,” he predicted to me, “both of us will score.”.

The next morning was overcast, and flurries of snow drifted to the ground as we huddled again around the kitchen stove. After breakfast George drove us to a spot close to where John had seen deer the day before. We had driven along that same trail several times before. Only two days before, John noted, the only track on the fresh snow had been made by a wandering coyote. Now deer tracks were everywhere.

It has been revealed that george left John and me where the road forked. He would pick us up late in the afternoon at a point about two miles farther on.

Industry observers note that few thrills can match walking through woodlands that you know contain game. You are tense and excited, and it’s difficult to slow down and hunt carefully enough.

In a recent development, john and I had scarcely separated when I saw deer running over an open ridge ahead and above me. I didn’t spot any antlers, but no matter. All the animals were out of range and gone before I would have had a shot.

It has been revealed that “Slow down,” I mentioned to myself half-aloud. But my pulse was racing.

That day I saw as many muleys as I’ve ever seen on a day’s hunt afoot. We had found a winter deer yard, and collecting venison would have been incredibly easy. But I kept hoping for the major buck. Actually I did see two together, but they were traveling and already 400 to 500 yards away.

It has been revealed that at dusk when I came out again on the road, weary to the bone, I still hadn’t fired a shot. The headlights of George’s vehicle were a welcome sight in the gloom. Even better was the big buck lashed on top. John had scored, and back at the ranch he told about it.

Sources indicate that early in the morning, after his eagerness had spooked a very good buck, John decided to hunt more from the seat of his pants and less by hiking all over the landscape. When he found a good sheltered place, he sat down on a deadfall. Though the mountain slope opposite him seemed empty of game, he studied it through his glasses. Soon he focused on a spike buck, bedded and almost hidden behind a juniper bush. John shifted his gaze slightly upward, and there he saw the kind of buck he wanted.

It has been revealed that the four-pointer was bedded in a cluster of trees and was in deep shadow. But his antlers, outlined against the snow, gave him away. John figured that the range was more than 500 yards — much too far to risk a shot — but that by making good use of the cover on his side of the mountain he could cut the distance in half. He made the stalk successfully, and one shot from his Model 700 Remington .30/06 anchored the buck.

That left one day — the last day of the open season — for me to score.

Perhaps because of the intense cold in the bunkhouse the next morning, the alarm clock didn’t work and George had to awaken me.

“Look out the window,” he called, “and over toward Canyon Creek.”.

In a recent development, there, in the crown of a dead spruce splintered long ago by lightning, sat the great gray owl. Probably another storm was on its way. As a result I wolfed my breakfast and, though I should have known better, got hooked on one of George’s cardboard pancakes.

In a recent development, george drove me close to the deer yard we had found, and from there I started out on foot. It was not a pleasant morning to be afield. Scattered snow flurries were being driven by a wild bitter wind, which was quickly obliterating deer tracks and which made cautious hunting — stopping often to scan the slopes — very difficult. I had to keep moving to keep warm. By mid-morning I had found very few fresh tracks and had seen no deer. I figured that all or at least most of the deer had already moved to even lower elevations ahead of the newly introduced storm. My chances looked very poor.

At noon I found some deadfalls on the edge of a dense spruce thicket that furnished a fairly good windbreak, and I sat down to munch a sandwich and a candy bar. The place also gave me a good view, between snow squalls, of distant, partly timbered mountainsides. Through binoculars I examined the wooded slopes, concentrating on those farthest away. As I glassed, I caught a slight movement much closer. Refocusing the glasses, I saw a forkhorn traveling slowly down the hill below me. He was less than 200 yards away, and though the crosswind wasn’t the best for shooting, it would not give me away.

In a recent development, I decided I would have to take the forkhorn or get nothing at all. Slowly I raised my rifle and found a rest for it on the deadfall. The shot would have been easy, but as I was about to squeeze off, a second forkhorn strolled out into the open. Then, right behind him, came a third buck.

At first I could see only the body of the third buck in my scope. But that was enough to tell me he was big. As I watched, the buck changed direction and was hidden from view again. Should I take a chance and play the waiting game, or shoot one of the forkhorns, still in sight?

The big buck resolved my indecision when he appeared again. This time I could see his splendid rack. My 7 mm. was sighted-in for 200 yards, so I held the crosshairs on the point of the shoulder, adjusted for windage, and squeezed. The deer lurched forward, out of view; I didn’t know whether I’d connected.

It has been revealed that I hurried down the steep slope and waded through a deep drift in a gully. I found the buck lying dead against a tree trunk. He was a fine four-pointer and as heavy a mule deer as I’ve ever bagged.

Recent findings suggest that that evening the great gray owl proved to be an accurate prophet. Another storm pounded the Rockies and plastered the high country with another layer of snow. But back at the ranch, I barely noticed it.

“The idea of the late hunt,” John stated, “was sure a great one.”.

A Montana nonresident major-game license costs $151. A deer-only license, which entitles the holder to one deer in a specified district, is $35, plus $1 for a conservation license. This year the general season on deer in Montana runs from October 22 to November 26. But prospective hunters should write the Montana Fish and Game Department, Helena, Montana 59601, for a copy of the detailed hunting regulations.

Read Next: I Promised to Take My Boys Rabbit Hunting Every Day of Christmas Break.

The tag end of the season can be a good time for any major-game hunt. Almost everywhere in the West, the odds for connecting with a trophy head may be improved then, simply because the animals are not so high and are easier to find. Of course, there are unseasonably warm years when animals are not driven downward by deep snow until after the season ends. Remember too that late-season hunting can be very rugged — and occasionally impossible. It’s wise to know bad-weather and snow-survival techniques. But these are the chances a sportsman must take. And for my money, the rewards are worth the gamble.

Latest Update: Barry Blanchard on His Many Lives, and the Tension Between Climbing and Family

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over five decades, Canadian alpinist Barry Blanchard has witnessed the evolution of climbing, summited major peaks around the world, and nearly died a few times –- not always in the mountains.
  • In the book, Blanchard avoids no topics or details about climbing, success, and failure, the struggle to combine adventure and family life, and how he has used up his nine lives.
  • Sources indicate that barry Blanchard speaks to ExplorersWeb’s Angela Benavides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over five decades, Canadian alpinist Barry Blanchard has witnessed the evolution of climbing, summited major peaks around the world, and nearly died a few times –- not always in the mountains. We caught up with the 67-year-old Canadian climber at the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival, where he presented his latest memoir, The Echo: Stories from the Edge of Survival.

In the book, Blanchard avoids no topics or details about climbing, success, and failure, the struggle to combine adventure and family life, and how he has used up his nine lives.

Sources indicate that barry Blanchard speaks to ExplorersWeb’s Angela Benavides. Photo: Jerry Kobalenko.

His latest comeback took place after he suffered a traumatic brain injury when he fell down a concrete stairway. “I had 11 skull fractures, and we didn’t know if I would ever be able to guide again or even climb or walk again, so [just in case,] my wife set me up to run a bed-and-breakfast,” he told Explorersweb.

ExWeb: How are you feeling now? Are you totally recovered?

It has been revealed that barry Blanchard: Yeah, the latest normal is great. Yeah, you know, about half the people with brain injuries [similar to what I had] don’t survive, so I have nothing to complain about.

I’ve lost a bit of the executive function, basically, the ability to hold three concepts in my mind at the same time. So I’m below Canadian standards with that, but on the other levels of the pyramid, I’m above Canadian standards.

We’re sure it’s been a long, painful process. What were the main challenges during the recovery period? You lost your memory for a while, didn’t you?

In a recent development, yeah, I had no memory for 13 days; it’s all gone, and I doubt it will ever come back. Now I feel I’ve been cursed with a long memory for long-term events, which was really good for my writing, but my short-term memory during that time was a real challenge.

On top of that is the emotional challenge. As my wife and my daughters pointed out, I was really good at acting like I was okay and talking to people as if I was okay, but they knew I wasn’t okay. It took time, effort, and lots of professional help to recognize and explain to my loved ones how I couldn’t cope with much, that I was not prepared to do what they wanted me to. I learned to say: “I have to finish this thing and then I will move on to the thing you want me to do. But I can’t do it right at the moment.”.

Industry observers note that how about your balance? As a climber and a guide, that’s pretty vital.

My doctor told me that balance would take the longest to return, and it was true. Initially, I started back in the climbing gym, always on top rope. But soon after going to the climbing gym, I started to go outside. The first thing I did was ice climbing — luckily, with some of the best ice climbers in the world belaying me from above.

Industry observers note that barry Blanchard climbing in the Canadian Rockies in 2022. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard.

It has been revealed that on one of the early climbs, I nearly fell over [due to poor] balance. I talked to the people at the hospital, and they pointed out that the brain is 2% of the body mass but it needs 20% of the oxygen. So they gave me a great tip: to stop and breathe. When I feel I am losing balance, I stop and focus on deep breathing for five or 10 minutes. It works.

Sources indicate that also, for a couple of years, the moment I touched the rock, I’d get vertigo, so I just learned to wait for 30 seconds or so till the vertigo passed, and then I could climb. Now that’s gone.

Overall, It’s been an interesting voyage, but I can’t recommend it. Do not get a traumatic brain injury. I don’t know if you have had one, but don’t.

What a twist of fate, after decades engaged in objectively risky climbs, that your closest call was a domestic accident…Do you often reflect on that?

Recent findings suggest that I identified this a long time ago: It’s great to be good at what you do, but you also need luck. The accidents I’ve had in the mountains, I’ve had enough good luck that things worked out. But just adding a little bit of bad luck to those situations, I wouldn’t be here, such as on Howse Peak* in 1999, as I was about to turn 40. If I’d have been six inches farther exposed to the avalanche, I wouldn’t be here.

According to recent reports, but you know, there’s some skill involved in that, and my buddy put a good anchor under a little bulge of limestone. The ice screw got ripped out in the avalanche, but the piton held. I was lucky.

The east face of Howse Peak in 1999. Photo by Blanchard’s climbing partner, Steve House.

[Note: Howse Peak*, located in Banff National Park, is also the peak where David Lama, Jess Roskelley, and Hansjorg Auer lost their lives in an avalanche in 2019. According to Blanchard, the accident was bad luck.].

According to recent reports, in your upcoming memoir, you are extremely honest about your struggle to combine your climbing and personal life. How hard is to be an alpinist and a family man?

Industry observers note that I divide my life into four quarters, as in Canadian football. In my first two quarters, almost all was about my passion for alpinism and my belief in it unconditionally. It was my church. In that time, my first marriage ended, and I got a divorce largely because of the tension between alpinism and being a husband, and also not being a loyal husband.

Recent findings suggest that as I explain in the book, my wedding ring was on one hand, and my ice axe was in the other, and I was being kind of pulled apart. My second marriage has also ended, but it gifted me the birth of my two daughters. I was also at the most effective point of my life as an alpinist around 33 to 35.

Then, some things start to change within the body. My reflexes slowed down, and so did my ability to adapt to high altitude. As testosterone decreased, the responsibility of fatherhood increased. Having a daughter changed my point of view about risk and risk tolerance.

Soon after she was born, I was in the Coast Range with my climbing partner from Colorado, Mark Wilford, doing a route on the north face of Bravo Peak. I couldn’t tell whether the snow would stick to 50-55º steep slopes, because it was a maritime snowpack, which is different from the continental snowpack we were used to climbing on at home. [In the Canadian Rockies,] you just don’t get snow sticking like that. Every time we moved a foot or a hand climbing up that type of snow, we were making a judgment about avalanche risk. Every time I made those decisions, I saw Rosemary’s face. It really changed my risk tolerance quite a bit.

Blanchard is back to climbing and guiding. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard.

I heard recently that in the 1970s, Formula 1 drivers won because they were totally prepared to die. And of the 20 Formula One drivers at that time, typically one would die every year. Is that the attitude you have to have going in and how you deal with fear? It’s like, okay, if it happens, it happens, and I’m perfectly okay with it?

In the late ’70s, early ’80s, we used to have a saying among ourselves, kind of joking, but it came true for some of my fellow alpinists: “I’m glad we didn’t die, now we can try something harder.”.

Now, being a father is the most important thing for me.

Over decades of climbing around the world, you have seen expeditions evolve from pioneering ascents to the huge commercial expeditions on Everest. From your point of view, what has changed and what remains the same?

The thing that is the same is the experience inside the alpinist, at the heart of the alpinist, and the fear of falling. That fear doesn’t change. And what has changed over time is technology: it’s easier to stay warm, it’s easier to go lighter, we have far better ice tools and ice screws, all that stuff.

Recent findings suggest that we do climb harder now; we climb faster, we climb steeper, thanks to modern training methods. Weather forecasts are so good now, but the heart of an alpinist and the fear remain. In fact, one of the gifts of alpinism is that you learn to make fear an ally. That fear is your body demanding more security. If you allow your fear to progress to panic, you’re going to fall.

It has been revealed that blanchard on Nanga Parbat in 1988. Photo: Courtesy of Barry Blanchard.

You are of Métis heritage. How have your indigenous roots shaped your relationship to mountains and nature?

I’m Métis, which is a separately identified culture in Canada. We’re a mixed breed, basically half European, half indigenous. The indigenous side of my bloodstream allows me to look at nature and perceive I am related to everything: the trees, the rocks, the mountain…Everything is alive, nothing is dead, everything has a spirit.

I’ve had some really powerful spirits in my life. In 1980 in Chamonix, after the hardest climb that my buddy Kevin [Doyle] and I did, we were down in our illegal campground in the Chamonix Valley, and I leaned my back against a large tree and wrapped my arms around the sides. Then I felt the ancestor in the tree, and that ancestor told me to dedicate my life to alpinism. It happened right there; that’s when I made the decision. And now, one of my really important ancestors is the mountain that is the namesake of our guiding firm. Colonists call it Yamnuska, but the Stony Nakoda people call it Îyâ Mnathka (pronounced Iyamunushka) — which translates to “flat-faced mountain.”.

Industry observers note that I’ve spent over 500 days of my life on Îyâ Mnathka, who is a very important ancestor for me. In particular, there is one tree that I’ve been touching and standing around and even anchoring off of for over 40 years — and it’s a tough place on top of this mountain to make a living as a tree. When I go to the mountain, I offer tobacco to the land at the base of the mountain and ask for permission. And then when I get to the rock, I touch the rock and take some time to just feel it and communicate with that ancestor before I leave. Sometimes the ancestor is good to me, and sometimes it’s not, like all mountains.

It has been revealed that that’s why I hate the word “conquering” applied to heading up on Everest in the conga line. If you get to the top, it’s because that ancestor allows you to get to the top. There’s nothing conquered about it.

You have worked in several mountain-related Hollywood films as a climbing double or safety advisor, including the recent Tenzing film, by Jennifer Peedom. Please tell us about it.

According to recent reports, I’m really proud of this one. It’s differently from what I felt after Cliffhanger or Vertical Limit, films in which I also participated. On Tenzing, I was the mountain safety officer. I was actually teaching Willem Dafoe and Tom Hiddleston, who play Hillary, about climbing in 1953 climbing equipment.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, I had to leave the role because my ninth cat life got used up in New Zealand. I lost an edge skiing on a very frozen surface and took a bad fall and suffered a few fractured bones.

In fact, Blanchard has had so many surgeries, replacements, and metal pieces in his body that he considers himself one of the best owners of Canada’s public health system.

Tech Report: Hunting Unpressured Bucks on One of the Best Properties in the Country

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we are well into deer season now, and bucks are definitely feeling the pressure. If you’re like the rest of us, you’re probably seeing daylight movement start to decrease on your trail cameras, or maybe it’s already dropped off. I’m right there with you. The places that I hunt see plenty of pressure, even though they’re on private ground. This week on the podcast, I’m talking to our gear editor, Scott Einsmann, who just came back from an incredibly unique experience: He was hunting almost completely unpressured mature bucks in the Midwest. Scott shares what that experience was like, what he learned from it, and how it can help him — and you — back in the real world of deer hunting. —Alex Robinson, editor-in-chief.

Listen to this episode on Apple, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Alex Robinson: Hey, Scott, thanks for joining the Outdoor Life Podcast. I want to talk to you about your favorite thing in the world, which is bowhunting for whitetail deer.

According to recent reports, scott Einsmann: Awesome. Let’s do it. I just came off the most amazing week of bowhunting for whitetails.

Sources indicate that alex: Yeah. We’re coming up on the holiday season, and you have a good redemption story, and everybody loves a good redemption story around the holidays. So to start this off, explain the property that you’re able to hunt in Illinois. What’s it like, and how did you weasel your way into getting bowhunting access to this place?

Scott: It’s 800 acres in southern Illinois, and what makes it a really good 800 acres is, one, it has topography, and it also has large wood blocks in it, and it’s surrounded by major ag fields. So once all the crops are cut, all the deer get sucked right into this property. For that reason, it’s just insane hunting. There are really good deer. There’s not a 200-incher on it, but there are a ton of 130- to 150-inch deer, and a ton of really good 8-points — some really cool deer. Last year, some big 6-points were killed, which is always fun. And maybe 300 does just running around this place. I mean, it’s crazy.

Alex: So talk about whose property it is and how you’re able to get on it, because you’re not a multimillionaire property owner.

Alex: A lot of these properties are either owned or leased by — you know, it’s the stuff that everybody dreams about hunting, but not everybody really gets access to.

Scott: Yes. And I did inquire with the farm manager there: How does someone get a lease in this area? You really just have to know the local farmers, because a lot of them have been burned by people leasing their property and not treating it right. So you really have to have someone to vouch for you and then be part of the community.

Luckily, I know someone. Levi Morgan and Andy Morgan have the lease for this property, and they have several leases in the area now, and they’re all pretty incredible. But this one they’ve had the longest — about three years now — and they’re really starting to dial it in and understand how the deer use it. They’re connected with our friends at Tactacam Reveal, and part of being an outdoor writer is you get to go on press trips.

In a recent development, press trips vary in quality and fun. But this one is by far the best I’ve ever been on, because it’s not a guided hunt. You’re not just being driven around by an outfitter and sitting over a corn pile somewhere. We go out there in the summer, we hang stands, we hang cameras, get to learn the property a little bit, and then we have access to those cameras all season long — which for me is great, because my home lease is not that exciting by comparison.

Sources indicate that scott: So just being able to scroll and see cool deer after cool deer — and they have a ton of turkeys as well, and I have some good news there. So we have access to all that, and then we come back in November and hunt the place during the peak of the rut.

And it is so much fun to be in a place where you get to see whitetail deer acting like whitetail deer, because it gets hunted two weeks out of the year, by bowhunters only. There’s no gun hunting on it. So it’s a substantial property with very limited pressure, and these deer act like deer. They’re out in the middle of the day. There’s this one field right by the hog barn, and there’s a little strip of beans in it, but the rest is wheat or rye or something like that. It’s a huge field. At 1 o’clock in the afternoon on any given day, there’s a dozen does out there, and there’s probably going to be a buck checking every one of those does. It’s a really hard place to kill a deer, but it’s a fun place to watch deer.

It has been revealed that it’s just an example. There are just deer out like that. In my area, in the Southeast, you would never see that, because someone’s going to take a shot at those deer from the road.

Alex: Yeah, I mean, even my area of Wisconsin and Minnesota — you’ve got a couple people hunting every, say, 80 acres, right? If you split up all the farmland around my area of western Wisconsin, there’s probably one hunter per 80 acres hunting pretty much every weekend. Some of those guys are very good hunters and they’re holding out for significant bucks. Other folks are just out there for fun and they’re going to shoot whatever. There’s a lot in between, but there is hunting pressure basically from October through the heart of the gun season, which we’re in right now.

Industry observers note that we have private property in north-central Wisconsin that my family always hunts, and opening day of gun season, it’s like a war zone. You just hear gunfire from all directions echoing through the morning, basically that entire first day. You can see the neighbors on their properties. Some folks will sit right on the property line. And even though we’re hunting private land, the deer know that they’re being hunted, and it’s a high-pressure situation. And that’s not even considering public land, right? So you have this view into a world that very few —.

Alex: Very few places even exist like this, where deer can just be deer throughout basically the fall cycle.

Scott: Yeah, pretty much. And I’m lucky to be at a place in my hunting career where I really, really appreciate it. I know how good it is and how lucky I am.

Industry observers note that alex: So this is your second crack at it this season. And not to dredge up the dark times, but I feel like enough time has passed now: You hunted out there last season. Talk about what went down.

In a recent development, scott: So last season, one, we didn’t hit the chase period — the rut — as well as we did this year. So we weren’t really seeing a ton of deer, by the standards of this place in Illinois.

In a recent development, scott: This was maybe day three or so. I had sat a stand on this cool little food plot that we have down there, and some guy just ends up walking in on the setup around 8 or 9 o’clock in the morning.

Alex: Like, trespassing into it?

Scott: Yes, trespassing into it. I took a picture of him real quick and shot a text to Levi and Andy, who had already killed their deer, so they were just helping everybody else kill. They mentioned they would be there lickety-split. We said hi to the guy, and he looked up like a doe who just realized that you were there. Just busted. And he said, “Oh, sorry,” and then he left. I was like, “That was so weird. I don’t know who that was or what they were doing here.”.

And it turns out that in Andy and Levi’s truck was the farm manager, John, who is a character all of his own. We should do a documentary about him. He’s such an interesting individual. So they’re pulling in, and they see this guy leaving where we’re at. Before the truck even stops, John is out of the truck running up to this guy, and he just unloads a verbal assault on him. Andy and Levi are in the truck in shock, like, “Oh my God, is there about to be a huge fight?” But this guy understood that he was in the wrong, and he backed off, apologized and left. Turns out he was living next door, and they believe he was being evicted, and they think he was coming to look for something to steal before he left.

Scott: Yeah. Luckily that didn’t happen.

Alex: So, like, maybe trying to grab some trail cameras or —.

Industry observers note that scott: Yeah, trail cameras or something, whatever. Not the most upstanding citizen of McLeansboro, Illinois.

According to recent reports, alex: OK. All right. So we’ve got this going on in the middle of your hunt.

Scott: Yeah. So that spot is blown, but I’m watching trail camera feeds nonstop. And that morning, there was a good deer in this food plot just up the hill from where we were sitting, and we had seen him from that spot. They were like, “He might come back there this evening. Let’s try to get into that stand.” So we get up there. It’s called Liquid Death, and it’s right next to a plot called Andy’s Plot. So you have these two food plots that are right next to each other, and right behind the stand you have a really nice watering hole.

It has been revealed that we see some does throughout the day into the evening, and then it’s the last hour of daylight and we see a buck way off. There are some does right up on the hill that this food plot leads up to, and he bumps one of those does down. She comes down into the food plot pretty close to us, like 30-ish yards. And then he’s up there on this hill, sun going down, perfect golden-hour lighting, just looking unbelievably majestic. Oh, and by the way, I have a camera guy over my shoulder filming all this.

So then he follows that doe right down into the plot. I had ranged little empty spots in the food plot, or little shadows, earlier in the day, but now it’s last light. There are no shadows.

Scott: But also my brain was not working. I don’t know exactly what my thought process was, but I was at full draw, and I dropped my 35 pin behind the shoulder and shot. As soon as the arrow hit, it was like, ugh, because it did not penetrate even a little bit. You could just see it hanging out. And he bounds off and stands at 60 yards.

Industry observers note that scott: Yeah, a high shoulder hit. And he’s standing there right at 60, looking around, not sure what just happened. He stood there for a while, and then he just walks off into the woods. And I was just like, “What just happened?” I think everyone knows that thick feeling when you know you just screwed up major time — especially because it was a great deer, a really nice, tall 8-point.

Industry observers note that so what had happened is I shot him for 35, and he was 30. And looking back at the slow-motion footage, he dropped a few inches. Also, his leg that was closest to me was back, and that arrow hit the upper portion of the scapula — there’s that hard ridge right there. The arrow hit that bone square. So it didn’t even hit the soft part of the scapula, where you might have a chance. It hit right on that bone. I would imagine that deer survived. We looked all the next day, and we didn’t find anything but a few drops of blood.

Recent findings suggest that alex: Yeah, that’s a nonlethal hit with archery equipment pretty much every time. You’re just kind of screwed. That’s not where you want to shoot a deer, you know?

Scott: No. If you’re trying to kill one, that’s not the spot to hit them.

Scott: And to make matters worse, I’ve been a fan of archery my whole life, and Levi Morgan is the guy in 3D archery — definitely the greatest of the current generation, and in the conversation for greatest 3D archer of all time. And he’s across the field watching this with some other guys, and their binoculars all go down. Oh, no. So someone you look up to is watching you screw up. Even worse.

Alex: Yeah. And he has you on his property to hunt these big deer. And you’re like, “I’m an Outdoor Life archery guy. I can do this. I’ve bowhunted my entire life. This is my thing.”.

Recent findings suggest that scott: Yeah. And there were a lot of things I did wrong there, obviously. I think the moment was so big — this really cool sequence of events — and I just didn’t take the second to range. My rangefinder was right there. I could’ve just clicked and confirmed, but in the moment I was like, “Yep, that’s 35, maybe.” That little short circuit is ultimately what it was, because the shot-execution part was fine.

Alex: It’s not like you hit far back. You basically hit where you were aiming, right? You were just aiming with the wrong pin, or you were not holding low enough.

Industry observers note that scott: Yeah. It’s the dumbest of all mistakes to make.

Recent findings suggest that alex: Going back to the unpressured deer, one thing that I have noticed — especially with more mature bucks in the rut — is you can get away with so much more than we often think. Especially if you’re used to hunting deer earlier in the year, or shooting does, where any little movement or any little mistake and their attention is on you. There have been times where I’ve tried to stop a buck with the classic “meh” to get them to stop walking so I can shoot, and they’re 20 yards away and they don’t stop. I’ve had to yell to get their attention, because they’re just in that rut mode.

It has been revealed that and I guess my point is I’ve made mistakes of being in the tree and thinking, “OK, I can’t range. I need to just shoot, because if I try to range and then draw, he’s going to see me draw, and I just have to make this shot.” Oftentimes you can range. Even if the buck’s in the open, you can draw, and maybe they see you and stop and then you can shoot them, or maybe they don’t even see you.

It has been revealed that scott: Yeah. And it was also an open field, so it’s not like you could range some trees and have real landmarks — which I guess I’m not very used to. I don’t hunt a lot of open fields. But talking to Levi this year about what he does in the tree when a buck is coming in, he has his rangefinder in his hand and is ranging the deer as it’s coming in, thinking about all the possible places where that buck could end up in front of him. He’s one of the best people in the world at judging distance, and he’s still ranging the deer as it comes in until he gets a shot.

Industry observers note that alex: Yeah. A world-champion 3D archer is doing this.

In a recent development, scott: Yes. And he said he wants to know the exact distance that deer is at before he pulls back his bow.

Industry observers note that alex: On my tree harness, I have a little clip that I clip my rangefinder to, so I can range and then just drop it, and it stays on my harness. I don’t have to shove it back in my pocket or take it out. Honestly, I started doing that after a similar situation to yours. I shot a buck that was closer than I thought, and because of that, I didn’t hit him well and didn’t get him. And I was like, “OK, now I need to range every shot, unless it’s obviously 20 yards or closer.”.

Scott: Yeah. And I’ve also started aiming a little lower. I was aiming mid-body behind the shoulder, but now I’m aiming at the top of the heart, especially on those closer shots.

Sources indicate that alex: OK. So let’s move to this year. What was your hunt like this year? How’d that play out?

According to recent reports, scott: So this year, we hit a cold front just as we were arriving. It was pretty incredible, actually, to have that timing — perfect weather, ideal conditions. The deer were chasing. You could see it all on the trail cameras from 10 a.m. until 3 p.m. Bucks everywhere.

Scott: The day that we arrived, we were planning on trying to get out in the stand. We all got there around noon, but we were like, “We can’t, because there are deer everywhere and we’ll just end up bumping them. It’s better to sneak in in the morning and then hunt.” And so that’s what we did.

One really cool thing that I’ve learned from Levi and Andy is how to hunt deer without them knowing that they’re being hunted. They are very particular about their entry and exit routes into the stands — getting in clean, getting out clean, in terms of wind direction, ground scent and just not bumping deer on your way to a stand location. So they have some really cool, sneaky spots where you can very easily get in and get out.

The one I was hunting, there are these train tracks that run through a portion of the property, and they have three stands right off the train tracks. You drive a side-by-side down the train tracks, go maybe 50 yards into the woods, and you’re up a tree. So it’s real easy, with no chance of really bumping anything, and you just sit there all day. For the most part, they’re on pinch points between food and bedding, or on natural travel corridors. I mean, there isn’t a bad spot on this property, but these ones in particular are very, very cool.

Alex: I have a quick question on that. You have all this camera activity and you’re getting pictures of all these bucks, and obviously some places are going to be a little harder to access than others. And then you have these train-track stands that are super sneaky to get in and out of. I feel like I know the answer to this, but if there’s one camera that has a giant buck on it, but there’s a probability of spooking deer on that access, versus these other cameras where you know you can get in clean and out clean — which one are they going to send you to?

Scott: The ones you can get in and out clean.

Alex: Even though you only have a few days to hunt, they’re like, “No matter what, we’re not going to spook deer.”.

Industry observers note that scott: Pretty much. For example, that stand I hunted last year — this year, Levi shot a really nice buck out of that same stand. And right after that, there were more big bucks on that same food plot every single day. But nobody hunted it, because you can’t get in there in the morning without bumping them. It’s a food plot, and the only access is to walk down the edge of the woods. The other problem is the wind direction ended up switching. So you’d have to try to get in there in the middle of the day, but the deer were so active in the middle of the day that that whole really awesome spot with good deer on it didn’t end up being huntable.

According to recent reports, another part of this approach is they’re really hunting the outer perimeter of the property and not going right into the middle. Last year we had trail cameras down in these creek bottoms, and it was like a deer highway, especially in the middle of the day — big bucks just cruising up and down. But we didn’t hunt them, because there’s too great a chance of getting busted in there. When the thermals switch, the wind has to be so perfect that it’s not worth the risk of going right into the middle of the property and trying to kill a deer, because you’re going to blow the whole property out on that one attempt. Maybe if it was just your property you could do whatever you want, but there are other people trying to kill bucks at the same time.

Alex: So the reason the deer are the way they are is, one, because it’s only hunted two weeks out of the year. But two, the way that it’s hunted, the deer don’t even feel the pressure that they have on them, because they’re just not bumping into humans or human scent.

Scott: Right. And in the places where they are — I mean, it’s an active farm. They’re used to seeing people on the farm roads and stuff.

Alex: OK. I’m starting to get it.

Scott: And just to hit that point a little bit more: When you do bump a deer going in, if you’re accessing through an area where they’re used to seeing people, those deer will be right back.

Industry observers note that alex: Yeah. It’s not like you’re bumping them out of their bedding area or their main feeding area. Got it. All right, go on with your hunt for this year.

According to recent reports, scott: So back to the redemption day. I’m in this stand. Another thing about hunting with Levi and Andy is they like to hang their stands very high. One of the guys got into one and ranged it, and it was 12 or 13 yards to the bottom of the tree. So like 36 feet in the air. They’re not all that high, but they’re all at least 20 feet up.

Sources indicate that alex: Why do they do that? For scent, or so you don’t get seen, or they just like it?

Scott: A little bit of both. I talked to Levi about this last year. It’s just how he grew up hunting. His dad always hung the stands really high, because he’s from North Carolina, where deer actually do look up into trees as they walk. So this is what he’s used to and what he’s always done. And Levi’s also really tall. He’s 6-foot-4. So if you’re shorter than 6-foot-4, you might have to make some jumps as you climb up the sticks, because of the gap between the sticks. Luckily I didn’t have that problem.

Alex: OK. So somehow you made it way high up there.

In a recent development, scott: I’m high up in the tree. I’ve got a camera guy with me, and the stand looks higher than it is because it’s up on a hill, and you’re looking down at a couple trails that are at the bottom of this hill. So it’s a pretty steep downward angle.

According to recent reports, the morning was pretty quiet for the most part. That first hour of daylight, I saw some deer, nothing crazy. Saw a coyote. Heard the most amazing turkey vocalizations of all time — a huge group of hens behind us, everything in the book. It was nuts, and loud. So that was cool for me. And then we had an 8-point come in at about 15 yards — a really nice, maybe 3-year-old typical 8-point. But the camera guy couldn’t get on him. And I mean, it’s the first morning.

Alex: Let’s see what else is out there.

Scott: Yeah. I’m not used to passing a deer like that, but I did. It felt weird. And the morning just goes on. We hear some deer fighting behind us. I see some bucks cruising the ridge ahead of us, about 100 yards out. And then it goes quiet, and I start eating every snack and sandwich I packed. Getting a little sleepy — it’s 12 o’clock, the sun’s on me. I’d packed a heavier jacket, so I throw it on, and I’m kind of nodding off, not really paying attention.

According to recent reports, and then all of a sudden, the woods erupt in front of us, and two does come barreling down into this bottom. I’m trying to get my stuff together and stand up out of this — I was in a Millennium stand, so I was very comfortable — trying to sit up and grab my bow off the hanger. And then I’m looking for whatever buck is going to be coming in after them.

Industry observers note that alex: Can I ask you a quick question? When you have deer come in and you’re pretty sure it’s a buck, do you stand up or do you stay sitting down?

According to recent reports, scott: In this stand, because of the shot angle, you definitely had to be standing to bend over for that shot. But the year before, there was a limb that came up right where my top cam was, so I had to sit and shoot, which I’m not used to.

So I get stood up. There are some deer coming off to the left now. I see another doe come running in, and I’m looking for the buck that’s chasing these. And then I see this tall 8-point that has tines that almost come in and touch. He’s the one that I had seen on the trail cameras leading up to this trip. I’d actually talked to Levi about him the day before, as we were discussing all the cool deer: “Man, I really, really like that unique 8-point look.” And it’s him — on the complete opposite side of the farm from where I had seen him the day before.

Sources indicate that scott: Yep. So he’s coming in. I had ranged some trees ahead of time, and there are pretty much two trails he could have walked in on: one that goes from 30 to 20 yards in front of the stand, and one that goes right under the stand. He’s standing right by the one that goes from 30 to 20, and I know I’m going to shoot him with either my top pin or my second pin. So I come to full draw, thinking he’s going to step out and turn broadside any second. And he’s just standing there, and I’m at full draw thinking, “What is this dude going to do?” And he turns and walks to the closer trail, which none of the does had walked in on.

Recent findings suggest that now he’s going to be coming in about 10 yards from me. I’m at full draw for what felt like forever, but it was totally fine, with a giant buck in front of me. He’s walking, and I give him the bleat, and he does not stop. I do a louder one, and then he stops, and I drop my top pin just above the midline on his body, since it’s such a steep angle. And the shot goes off. I was shooting a resistance release, and it went off very easily. And I see about half an arrow’s worth of penetration, and I’m like, “Not again.”.

Recent findings suggest that alex: Oh, no. Did it feel like you hit where you aimed?

Scott: I honestly don’t remember. I’m just glad it was 10 yards. Maybe we got lucky there. The deer runs off, and then we hear him crash. I’m looking at the camera guy, and I’m not ready to celebrate, because I’m not feeling 100 percent confident in the shot. Typically I’m used to passing through deer, with either compounds or recurves, especially at that distance. But we heard him crash, so I felt pretty good about it.

Recent findings suggest that it takes me a while to settle down, and we climb down. I don’t find any blood where I shot him, but we start walking in the direction we heard him crash, and there he was, lying there 40 yards away — dead as a doornail.

Scott: Basically what happened is the arrow came in high, right behind the shoulder, and then exited at the armpit on the offside and hit the elbow bone on that offside shoulder.

Alex: And that’s what stopped it.

According to recent reports, scott: Yeah. The broadhead was just poking through the skin on the offside. So luckily he crashed close, because that would’ve been a tough one to track.

Alex: So basically two years of hunting this place, and you walk up on this deer. You made your shot. How does that feel?

Sources indicate that scott: It took me a while for it to fully sink in, because hunting in the rut, things happen so quickly. I was about to take a nap, and two minutes later this deer is there. It was a huge weight off my shoulders. I got to have a drama-free experience of finding the deer. Everything went great on that end. And then Levi and Andy came in the side-by-side, we picked him up, and it was just like, “Man, what a relief.” But at the same time, I was like, “I really want to spend more time in this stand.”.

The day after, I couldn’t get into the stand to try to fill my doe tag, but I ended up hanging stands with Levi and Andy on one of their fresh leases, and that was awesome. We found such a cool spot, and I got to watch how they approach picking a tree and that on-the-run scouting. I mean, that was worth the price of not going hunting that day. I would much rather do that.

According to recent reports, alex: What was your biggest takeaway from watching those guys? They know an area’s good, but what’s the next step for narrowing it down to, “OK, this tree is where we’re going to hang it”?

Sources indicate that scott: Andy calls it structure, because he’s a pro bass fisherman, so it’s terminology he’s familiar with. Basically what they’re looking for is little things that will funnel deer movement closer to your stand location, but also give you a backstop for your wind direction — like, deer won’t be coming from here, so we can hunt it on this wind. The way he puts it is you’re always giving up something. There’s not one perfect wind direction. You always have that risk, but you’re trying to minimize it and at the same time funnel deer past your stand location.

In this case, there’s an ag field maybe 60 yards in front of the stand. Then in the woods behind you, there’s a really thick brier patch that deer won’t walk through. But there’s an opening in the brier patch, and an old two-track that comes in also. You could just see the deer trails funneling right through this spot that they found. Then you find the right tree to hang it in. It was cool. We saw a couple of really good deer while we were hanging that stand, so it’ll be a good one for next year. But those guys are always hanging more stands. I think they must have hung a few while we were there — more wind-direction options.

Sources indicate that alex: You had this whitetail wonderland experience, but what do you think your main takeaways are coming back to the real world and hunting regular places like the rest of us? What’s applicable?

Industry observers note that scott: I mean, the entry and exit thing is something that I’ve applied to how I hunt my lease. I wish my lease neighbor did the same. But just being mindful of the pressure you’re putting on it going in, going out, and while you’re in the stand — where your scent cone is blowing.

It has been revealed that I still need to get better at staying present and task-focused when a big buck comes barreling in on you. Hunting during the rut can definitely leave you a little flat-footed sometimes. I think that’s just more experience than anything else, because I’m more used to hunting deer over food sources, where you have a little more time to get warmed up to the idea of killing this deer.

Alex: Right. So many times in the rut, you hear a buck coming, then you see him for a few seconds, and then you have to shoot. You have to decide that he’s a buck you want to shoot, and you have to decide how you’re going to shoot him and where, all in a matter of a few seconds. And like you said, you could’ve been about to take a nap or eat a sandwich 30 seconds before that, you know?

In a recent development, scott: Yeah, for sure. And I got pictures last night of a really great deer on my lease. I mean, it was 9:30 at night, but I still have another month to find that deer and get him killed.

Alex: All right, Scott. Well, thank you for the insight and for sharing this little window into the perfect corner of whitetail hunting country. We can all live vicariously through you.

Scott: Yes. If I never get invited back, I won’t be too sad.

Latest Update: 3 Totally Normal Deer Hunting Tactics We Used to Think Were Utter Nonsense

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When they were first introduced to the national hunting community, these novel methods for bringing in bucks were considered unconventional at best, and harebrained schemes by most. Now deer hunters everywhere use these tried-and-true tactics. We take a look back to when these trusty standbys were still considered downright bizarre.

In a recent development, the brush-country hunters of Texas and New Mexico were crashing antlers together for decades before the trend caught fire in the rest of whitetail country. Although Native hunters almost certainly developed the technique, legend has it that an old market hunter accidentally discovered the phenomenon.

According to recent reports, “He was coming to town one day, his wagon loaded with deer carcasses, when a buck came barging out of the mesquite,” reads one May 1951 story from OL. “The hunter, so the story goes, added him to the load. A short time later, another buck pranced up — and was soon in the wagon. The puzzled hunter stopped to figure things out and discovered that two carcasses were lying so their antlers clashed as the wagon jounced along the rough country road.”.

Related: How to Rattle in a Buck, Based on Whitetail Deer Research.

Our first story devoted to rattling appeared in October 1937. A Texas game warden, drawing on 30 years of experience with the tactic, taught author Fredric P. Schwab exactly how to sound like “two bucks in a life-and-death struggle.”.

It has been revealed that by the 1950s, most hunters in the rest of the country had heard of rattling, but few had tried it. Almost everyone who had tried tickling tines reported the method didn’t work on hill-country deer, although a rare hunter outside the Lone-Star State would claim success. Here’s what modern research states about the efficacy of rattling in deer.

Industry observers note that the concept of calling for deer was less established even than rattling in the middle of the 20th century. In August 1949, an experienced deer hunter traveled to Alaska for a Sitka blacktail hunt. “He was sure it was just a gag,” reads the story. “Who ever head of calling a buck?”.

“Now I’ve used crow calls, duck calls, and turkey calls, and I’d read that down in Texas they lure bucks by rattling a couple of antlers together. But a real deer call I’d never heard of. Probably my voice expressed my skepticism. ‘O.K. I’ll bite. What’s a deer call?’”.

Read Now: When and How to Use a Grunt Tube to Call in Deer.

The Alaskan hunters employed the call often — which looks a bit like a harmonica and sounds like “a lost lamb bleating for its mother,” — but they admit they don’t know what sound it was supposed to replicate. “I’ve attracted does as well as bucks, so I don’t think it’s a mating call,” noted one local. “An old Indian told me it’s the cry of a fawn in mortal terror,” said another.

It has been revealed that in the end, the author and a fellow hunter call in two bucks and drop both of them. This story, “A Deer Call Brings ‘Em In!” garnered so much reader mail that an advice column on using commercial calls appeared in the August 1949 matter. The expert claimed to have used his call with excellent results on 100 wild deer, and that his call was a modern counterpart of those made by Native Americans in Alaska. So while calls were being produced commercially by the late 40s, they remained news to most hunters.

Although a variety of products designed to lure bucks and cover up human odor had been marketed for years, it appears most hunters initially considered the scents for sale at the local sporting goods shop akin to something hawked by a snake oil salesman.

Read Next: 15 Scent Control Strategies That Actually Work for Deer Hunting.

“It was probably because I was growing desperate that I decided to buy the deer scent,” writes John Weiss, author of the November 1978 feature “Scents and Nonscents.” “I figured there was nothing to lose.”.

Weiss reported that more than 50 companies made scents at the time, and were raking in an estimated $37 million a year. That included everything from hunter’s soaps and food attractants to tarsal scents and urine.

He then delved into the types of scents and their effectiveness, and dug into the “scientific” realm of deer hunting. Interestingly, most biologists interviewed for the story disregarded “a deer’s scenting ability as not all that vital.” One researcher noted that a deer’s “visual capabilities are far more refined than hearing or smelling abilities.”.

Yet most wildlife biologists today agree that a deer’s nose is it’s most formidable asset. Nonscents, indeed. It makes you wonder: If these are the facts we believed back then, just think about what we’ve got wrong now. And, even more fun to imagine, is what idiotic tactic might be all the rage in another couple decades.

In a recent development, this story, “‘Wacky’ Deer Tactics,” first appeared in the Oct. 2015 glitch of Outdoor Life.

8 Wild Fish and Game Recipes to Recreate the First Thanksgiving Dinner

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football.
  • “Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.
  • Sources indicate that that sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, pumpkin pie, and football. In America, that’s usually what’s on the menu on the fourth Thursday in November. But in the fall of 1621, the original Thanksgiving meal didn’t resemble this in the slightest. The Pilgrims at Plymouth Plantation had a lot to be thankful for. The Wampanoag helped them survive the previous winter and harvest plenty of food over the summer. The two groups decided to come together and celebrate this for a few days with a feast, during which they ate a mix of wild fish and game. Here is an excerpt from one of two firsthand accounts from a man named Edward Winslow:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the company almost a week. At which time, amongst other recreations, we exercised our arms, many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some ninety men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted, and they went out and killed five deer, which they brought to the plantation and bestowed on our governor, and upon the captain and others.”.

Sources indicate that that sounds a little more like deer camp than grandma’s house. Along with a pile of venison and week’s supply of fowl, it’s not out of the question to assume there were also dried fruits, berries, nuts, fish, and shellfish at the feast. Being that most of these things are available to hunters and anglers, we took a deep dive into some of our favorite recipes. In the spirit of that original Thanksgiving meal, here are eight ways to bring back some wild game to the table this season.

Industry observers note that the Wampanoag indicated the colonists a lot ways to grow and keep food, but neither group had access to refrigeration. Instead, things like berries and other fruit had to be eaten fresh or preserved. The most likely way they would have done this is by drying, but there’s another way to preserve fruit without refrigeration. Canning has been done for generations, and it’s still a perfect way to preserve wild berries for months. The pilgrims wouldn’t have had the sugar for this wild black raspberry jam recipe, but it still goes good with butter and toast, on a leftover turkey sandwich, or even some acorn-flour pancakes.

Today lobsters and other shellfish are considered delicacies, but 400 years ago, they were a staple. The Atlantic coastline provided Wampanoag and the colonists with clams, mussels, and lobster. But there’s also another crustacean, readily available in freshwater, that’s just as worthy of dipping in clarified butter: the crayfish. Here’s a classic crayfish etouffee to serve alongside the main course.

Industry observers note that in a heavy-bottomed pan, melt the butter and add the flour. You are going to make a roux: over medium heat, stir the roux until it darkens to the color of peanut butter (about 20 minutes). Add the onions, celery, and green peppers, stirring to combine. Add the garlic, tomato paste, and Worcestershire. Stir for a couple of minutes. Pour in the stock and the cooked crayfish tail meat. Stir for a few minutes until the roux in well incorporated into the stock and it starts to boil. Turn the heat down to a simmer, and add the Cajun seasoning. Then simmer for about 20 minutes until the etouffee thickens. Serve over wild rice or plain white rice. If you like yours a little hotter, add Crystal hot sauce or your favorite hot sauce.

In the first sentence of the Winslow account, there’s a mention of fowl:.

“Our harvest being gotten in, our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors.”.

Turkey is considered fowl, but the first thanksgiving probably included waterfowl instead. Ducks and geese would have been easier for the settlers and the Wampanoag to catch and cook. They are also more plentiful in the wild. The birds were most likely roasted over a fire. Spit roasting a whole bird is an involved process, and most will opt for an oven instead, given a chance. If you’re thinking about swapping duck for a turkey this year, this wild duck and squash curry is an excellent place to start.

Sources indicate that another bird readily available in the 17th century was the passenger pigeon. When populations were at their peak, it is noted that flocks were so thick they would black out the sky. Unfortunately, this didn’t last. Due to heavy market hunting and habitat loss, the passenger pigeon is now extinct. A similar bird (though not closely related) is the mourning dove. In fact, one of the last living wild passenger pigeons was found roosting with mourning doves.

A classic popper recipe will work with doves and most other upland birds (and it also pairs well with football). But most dove hunters already have that recipe figured out. Instead, here’s a flaky cheese and pepper dove roll recipe that’s sure to please.

Fish played a significant part in the colonist’s lives. They were loaned money to start the colony, and they planned to pay some of their debts back by fishing. Atlantic white cod would have been the fish of choice, though they would have also had access to other fish like runs Atlantic salmon. Here’s a linguini with salmon cream sauce recipe that makes use of the leftover, extra meat after filleting a fish.

It has been revealed that in a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat, add the shallots and garlic, and cook until soft (about 2 minutes). Season with a pinch of salt, and black pepper to taste. Add the wine and cook until almost all the wine is evaporated. Add the heavy cream and the parmesan and stir together, cooking until the cream thickens up a bit (1-2 minutes). Add the pasta and toss with the cream sauce. If the sauce is too thick, add some of the pasta water until you get a creamy sauce. Toss in the parsley, and serve topped with grated parmesan. This will make six healthy servings.

Industry observers note that so where did this turkey thing come from anyway? The one other written account from the autumn of 1621 does mention that the pilgrims had turkey, although nobody is certain that it was eaten at the feast. The second account from William Bradford states:.

“And besides waterfowl there was great store of wild turkeys, of which they took many, besides venison, etc.”.

It has been revealed that long after Bradford’s death, his journal was found and reprinted in the 1850s, and for some reason, people really liked the part about turkey. During that time, Sarah Josepha Hale, the editor of a magazine called Godey’s Lady’s Book, promoted the turkey as a centerpiece of the table. Hale was also a strong voice behind Thanksgiving Day becoming a national holiday. She wrote letters and even petitioned a few presidents.

According to recent reports, finally, in 1863, Abraham Lincoln declared the day a national holiday, and turkey has been the star of the show ever since. Whether wild turkey was eaten during the first Thanksgiving or not, it’s still delicious. If you have a left-over gobbler from the spring, or one you’ve shot this fall, this wild take on a classic Thanksgiving turkey recipe is sure to get some attention at your table.

• 2 gallons water • 2 oranges • 2 lemons • 1 onion, cut into 8 pieces • 1 cup brown sugar • 1 cup Kosher salt • Couple sprigs of fresh thyme or rosemary.

Make brining mixture, mixing all ingredients. Squeeze the oranges and lemons into the mixture and toss in the rinds too. Soak turkey in a cooler with ice and the brining mixture overnight. If you need more brine, use ½ cup salt and ½ cup brown sugar for every gallon of water. Use additional fruit as desired.

I lightly stuff the turkey with a couple celery stalks, onion pieces and a couple carrots, along with a half lemon and half orange from the brine mixture.
